Introduction to Generative AI: Beyond the Chat

Workshop 1 notes: learning to work with AI coding agents

This workshop took place on Friday, October 16, 2026, at Colorado State University. This page recaps the slides, gives a short overview of the live demo, and points you to other resources. Workshop 1 was designed for those with zero prior experience. If you want to go further, consider Workshop 2.

What is an AI coding agent?

Chat

You paste in what you want it to do and get code back. Then you copy it, run it, fix it, and paste it in again.

An agent

You say “clean this survey export and merge it with the state data,” and it opens the files, writes the script, runs it and checks the result.

The two main tools are Claude Code (Anthropic) and Codex (OpenAI). Everything from the workshop works in either one.

Why use one?

  • Write code fast. Go from a research question to code.
  • Handle the mundane. Hand off data cleaning, reshaping, merging and recoding variables.
  • Automate repetitive tasks. Run the same analysis across many datasets, models or specifications.
  • Lower the barrier to entry. Use tools you don’t have expertise in.
  • Apply best practices. Get guidance on standard errors, model diagnostics and robust specifications.
  • Improve replicability. The code it writes is commented and documented, so every step of the analysis can be seen.
Something to think about

Which tasks in your own work take the most time but the least judgment?

Think of AI as a research assistant

  • It’s fast, tireless, and good at routine tasks.
  • But it makes mistakes, so check its work.
  • It needs clear direction and correction.
  • It doesn’t always know what to do, and sometimes it tries anyway.
  • You are still the researcher. You’re responsible for the design, the interpretation and the conclusions.

Potential applications

Area Examples
Text and corpus work Word frequencies, concordances or topic comparisons across a folder of novels, speeches or interview transcripts
Messy data Cleaning survey exports, merging spreadsheets, fixing inconsistent coding
Document wrangling Renaming and organizing hundreds of PDFs or scans, extracting text, converting citation formats
Social science analysis Analysis scripts, with explanations
Writing Summarizing and interpreting results, and more

Ethical considerations

Data sensitivity

  • Your files stay on your computer, but anything the agent reads is sent to the model.
  • It isn’t always clear how secure the data is once it reaches the company.
  • You may not be allowed to share your data with an agent (for example, under your IRB protocol).
  • In the long run, models that run locally may solve this.

Disclosure and authorship

  • Most publishers say AI can’t be an author and that its use should be disclosed.
  • Disclosure norms are uneven and changing fast.
  • It’s also unclear how well people follow those norms.
  • You’re responsible for your work, whoever or whatever drafted it.

The workshop example

The goal was to work through a “complete” data project with an AI agent. Time was short, so treat what you saw as an introduction, not as best practice. The point was to give you enough understanding to explore further.

Research hypotheses and questions

Based on Gelman et al., Red State, Blue State, Rich State, Poor State (2008):

  1. Richer states vote more Democratic.
  2. Within states, richer people vote more Republican.
  3. The income gap in voting Republican is steeper in poor states than in rich ones.
  4. Did this change between 2020 and 2024?
  5. Does it depend on the respondent’s sex, race or education?

We used a 5,000-person sample per year from the Cooperative Election Study (CES), plus state median income (Census CPS) and state vote shares (MIT Election Lab).

Working with an agent

First steps

  • Work in a dedicated folder. The folder you start the agent in is its whole world.
  • You may need to grant permissions. It asks before editing files or running commands. Read what it asks before you approve.
  • Choose the model and effort level. Bigger models and more effort help with hard problems but are slower and use your allowance faster.
  • Give it standing context in CLAUDE.md (Claude Code) or AGENTS.md (Codex).

Memos

Write the project’s memory to files, not the conversation.

File Who it’s for What it holds
README.md / NOTES.md Humans What the project is and how it was built
CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md The agent How to behave in this project
PROGRESS.md Both Where things stand and what’s next

Context windows

Long conversations:

  • get muddled,
  • forget the original goal,
  • and can use up a lot of tokens.

Compact or clear. /compact summarizes the conversation so far. /clear (Claude Code) or /new (Codex) starts a blank one. Either way, use the memos: a fresh session can read NOTES.md and PROGRESS.md and pick up where you left off.

Quick reference: Claude Code vs. Codex commands
What you want Claude Code Codex
Start in the current folder claude codex
Standing instructions file CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md
Draft an instructions file /init /init
Choose model and effort /model, /effort /model
Change permissions Shift+Tab /permissions
Point at a specific file @file @file
See how full the context is /context /status
Summarize to free up space /compact /compact
Start a blank conversation /clear /new
Reopen an earlier session claude --resume codex resume

Both tools change often, so check the current documentation.

Overview of the demo analysis

The live demo ran in two sessions, with a /clear in between.

Session 1 got the data together. The agent read the CES file and flagged quirks (vote codes that mean different things in 2020 and 2024, “prefer not to say” coded as income). It found and downloaded state income and vote share data, merged everything, and organized the folder into data/, analysis/ and results/. Before stopping, we had it write NOTES.md and PROGRESS.md.

Session 2 began with “Where did I leave off?” From there it cleaned the data, produced descriptives, fit multilevel models, split the results by race, and ran robustness checks. It finished with a draft R Markdown report.

What we found, in brief: richer states voted less for Trump. Within states, the income pattern was weak. The steeper income gap in poorer states held up in the weighted models but was about half as large, and not significant, without weights.

The lesson

The agent made the analysis “easy” but deciding what it means is still your job.

Future steps

What would come next for a project like this:

  • Verification. Check results against numbers you already know, and open every source it cites.
  • More data and analyses. For example, ACS income in place of CPS, trimmed weights, or education interactions.
  • Further extensions.
  • Writing a paper: framing, literature review, data and methods, results.
